double-cheeseburger-on-wheat-bun-2-large.title: Double Cheeseburger on Wheat Bun, 2 Large Patties

content.title: About
content.content: The double cheeseburger consists of a wheat bun, two large beef patties (about 100 g each), two slices of cheddar cheese, lettuce, tomato, pickles, onion and sauce. It is a classic fast‑food item popular worldwide.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first cheeseburger appeared in the United States in the 1920s, and the double version became popular in the 1970s.
A wheat bun gives a softer texture compared to the traditional brioche.
Combining two patties with cheese raises the protein content to about 40 g per serving.
Cheddar is often chosen for its distinctive flavor and meltability.
Some restaurants serve the double cheeseburger with double sauce, increasing its calorie count.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Two beef patties provide roughly 40 g of protein, essential for muscle repair and satiety.

items.title: Source of iron and zinc
items.content: Beef is rich in heme iron and zinc, which support the immune system and metabolism.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheddar adds calcium, important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and cheese contain vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, aiding energy metabolism.

items.title: Dietary fiber from vegetables
items.content: Tomato, lettuce and pickles contribute a modest amount of fiber, beneficial for digestion.

items.title: High calorie count
items.content: One double cheeseburger contains about 800–950 kcal, which can contribute to weight gain if eaten frequently.

items.title: Saturated fat and cholesterol
items.content: Beef and cheese contain saturated fats that may raise cholesterol levels when consumed in excess.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: The sauce and cheese add a significant amount of sodium, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Cheddar may trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: Choose patties made from whole meat without fillers or excessive preservatives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the burger hot, split the bun, place the patties with melted cheese, add vegetables and sauce. It is typically eaten by hand, but a knife and fork can be used for a neater experience.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The burger is best eaten immediately. If you need to store it, cool it within 2 hours, then place in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat in an oven or grill to retain bun crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Boiled peanuts are shelled peanuts that have been cooked in salted water until tender. They have a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a soft‑crunchy texture. Boiled peanuts are enjoyed as a snack and are also used in salads, Asian dishes, and confectionery.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peanuts are legumes, not true nuts.
Boiled peanuts are a popular street‑food snack in the southern United States and parts of Asia.
They are botanically related to soybeans, beans, and peas.
Often they are boiled with aromatic spices such as garlic, paprika, and cumin.
Boiled peanuts can be processed into peanut butter, paste, and flour.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Peanuts provide about 25 % protein, making them a good plant‑based protein source.

items.title: Healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: Most of the fat in peanuts is monounsaturated, which supports heart health.

items.title: Source of vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative damage.

items.title: Contains magnesium and phosphorus
items.content: These minerals are important for muscle, nerve, and bone function.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber in peanuts aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanuts are one of the most common allergens and can cause severe reactions.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Peanuts are calorie‑dense, so portion size should be moderated.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking before boiling lowers its level.

items.title: Salt
items.content: Boiled peanuts are often salted; people with hypertension should choose unsalted versions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boiled peanuts can be eaten straight from the shell as a snack, added to salads, rice or noodle dishes, or used in sauces and spreads. They can also be ground into flour for baking or turned into homemade peanut butter.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store boiled peanuts in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life keep them refrigerated, where they stay fresh for 2–3 weeks. Discard any nuts that show mold, off‑odors, or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: A vegetable smoothie is a drink made from fresh vegetables, sometimes blended with fruit, water or plant‑based milk. It retains most of the vitamins, minerals and dietary fiber, providing a light yet nutritious way to stay hydrated and support overall health.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vegetable smoothies let you consume several servings of vegetables in a single drink.
Fiber content is usually higher than in juices because the pulp is not removed.
Adding leafy greens (spinach, kale) barely changes the taste but dramatically boosts iron and vitamin K levels.
A blend of carrot, beet and ginger is popular in detox programs for its antioxidant properties.
Cold‑served smoothies preserve more vitamin C than hot vegetable soups.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vegetables such as spinach and broccoli provide B6 and folate, supporting metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Beta‑carotene in carrots and lutein in leafy greens help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber from vegetables improves gut motility and promotes a healthy microbiome.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Vegetable smoothies are typically low in fat and sugar, making them suitable for weight management.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The high water content of vegetables helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Certain vegetables (spinach, beet) are high in oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Possible allergies
items.content: Rarely, some people may react to specific vegetables such as celery.

items.title: Nutrient loss with prolonged storage
items.content: Vitamin C and some enzymes degrade over time, so it’s best to consume the smoothie soon after blending.

items.title: Added sodium in commercial mixes
items.content: Pre‑made blends may contain added salt, which is undesirable for those with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink the vegetable smoothie immediately after preparation to retain maximum nutrients. Add protein powder, nut milk, or chia seeds for extra satiety. It can serve as a breakfast substitute, snack, or post‑workout recovery drink.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared smoothie in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size containers and thaw in the fridge before drinking.
